title: A Physics-Grounded QUBO Encoding of Irrigation Scheduling for QAOA
abstract: Rotational irrigation scheduling in water-scarce Central Asia is a densely coupled combinatorial problem: soil-moisture memory links each irrigation decision to all later days within a zone, field adjacency couples zones on overlapping window days, and rigid canal rotations quantize water delivery in time. We formulate it as a Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization (QUBO) by linearizing the root-zone water balance, so the quadratic crop-stress objective generates the physical couplings as 2-local Ising interactions with no higher-order terms; only the water-budget constraint requires an artificial all-to-all penalty, which we certify with an instance-adaptive weight bound an order of magnitude tighter than generic prescriptions. Every instance is built from observed data for a cotton district in Khorezm, Uzbekistan: NASA POWER meteorology, FAO-56 Penman--Monteith evapotranspiration, SoilGrids~2.0 hydraulics, measured capillary fluxes, and documented canal-rotation windows that enter as qubit-count reductions. We benchmark four tiers -- exact solvers, matched-budget heuristics, ideal-statevector quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA), and noise-model plus IBM Heron execution -- and add a scaling study on soil instances up to 584 variables. Exact branch-and-bound proves optimality in seconds through 150 variables, and heuristic degradation at fixed evaluation budget is repaired by scaling the budget, so no classical scalability wall appears at deployment-relevant sizes, and none is claimed. On hardware, the informative signal is optimum-sampling enrichment over uniform sampling. We claim no quantum advantage; we deliver a physically grounded, data-complete, reproducible encoding of a societally critical scheduling problem for the quantum-utility era.
summary: This paper tackles optimizing irrigation scheduling in water-scarce regions by formulating it as a QUBO problem. The authors successfully map the complex hydrological dynamics and operational constraints onto a 2-local Ising Hamiltonian suitable for QAOA. They emphasize that their primary contribution is providing a physically grounded, data-complete encoding rather than claiming quantum computational superiority.
main_problem: The paper formulates rotational irrigation scheduling, a complex combinatorial optimization problem, into a QUBO suitable for quantum computation.
main_result: They successfully map the physical constraints onto a 2-local Ising Hamiltonian, demonstrating that classical solvers can solve instances up to 150 variables quickly, and they claim no quantum advantage is demonstrated.
method: The core method involves linearizing soil-water balance dynamics and constructing a cost function composed of stress, budget, spatial, and timing penalties, which are then mapped to an Ising Hamiltonian for QAOA execution.
model_or_system: The system models water delivery in agricultural zones over time, governed by soil moisture memory. The optimization is framed as minimizing a QUBO/Ising Hamiltonian derived from hydrological equations using observed field data from Uzbekistan.
key_observables: Optimal irrigation schedule (binary decision vector $x_{z,d}$), total cost function value, and performance metrics comparing exact solvers vs. QAOA outputs.
important_parameters: Problem size scales up to 584 variables; the optimization is constrained by a finite water budget ($K$); quantum hardware tested includes the ibm_fez backend.
main_assumptions: Key assumptions include linearizing the soil-water balance (Assumption 1) and using symmetric quadratic penalties for stress, which are necessary to achieve a 2-local Hamiltonian structure.
figures_summary: The notes do not detail figure contents, but mention benchmarking tables (Table II, Table III) detailing parameters for small, medium, and large instances tested across various solvers.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the physical problem, derives the QUBO formulation by linearizing dynamics, details the mapping to a 2-local Ising Hamiltonian, benchmarks performance against classical methods (MIQP), and finally tests execution on quantum hardware using both standard QAOA and an XY-mixer variant.
why_interesting: While not directly about AMO physics, the rigorous process of translating complex physical constraints (like hydrology) into a mathematically structured Hamiltonian is highly relevant for developing quantum algorithms for real-world scientific modeling beyond simple toy models.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Classical scaling study on the real-soil instance ladder. (a) Mean optimality gap (20 seeds) of matched-budget SA and GA (2×104 evaluations), GA at 10× budget, and the greedy operational rule, relative to the proven optimum (n ≤150) or the best-known solution (n = 295, 584). (b) Exact MIQP time-to-optimality; crosses mark the license-capped fallback solver hitting its 900-s limit without a proof. Fixed-budget heuristic degradation is a budget artifact (the 10×-budget GA restores near-optimality), and certified exact solution remains fast through n = 150: no classical wall is observed at these sizes.

Fig. 1. Ideal QAOA depth scan. (a) Normalized approximation ratio of the energy expectation; dotted/dashed gray lines mark the SA mean over 20 matched-budget seeds for the small/medium instances. (b) Probability of sampling the exact optimum; uniform baselines are 2−11 and 2−21.

Fig. 3. Root-zone available water trajectories for the small instance, driven by observed 2024 Khorezm forcing; dotted lines mark the targets Tz and shaded verticals the irrigation events. (a) Exact optimum: triage — zones 1 and 2 are dosed before their windows close and zone 3 is deliberately sacrificed. (b) Greedy FAO-trigger rule: the depletion trigger fires only after the windows of zones 1 and 2 have closed; one dose goes to zone 3 and the second is never spent, leaving a 48.7% optimality gap.

Fig. 4. Approximation ratio of the sampled energy on the small instance: ideal statevector, transpiled circuits under shot noise only, the calibrated FakeFez (Heron r2) noise model, and IBM Heron hardware (ibm_fez; the L=1 point is the mean of four repeat executions). Noise inverts the benefit of depth.
